title: Effects of crude oil on the somatic and immune development of juvenile threespine stickleback
content:
by Kelly S. Ireland, Kathryn CA. Milligan-McClellan

Aquatic oil spills have profound effects on surrounding ecosystems, prompting significant investments in oil spill response efforts to remove oil from the environment as quickly as possible. Oil has immunotoxic effects and may be particularly harmful to larval and juvenile fish as it can cause a number of developmental defects and stunted growth. In spite of significant efforts to clean up oil, it is unclear whether larval and juvenile fish can recover from the effects of oil, and no work has been published on the effect crude oil has on developing threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) fish. Threespine stickleback are a ubiquitous sentinel species in the Northern Hemisphere and an important food source for many larger, economically valuable fish. As fish with fully marine, anadromous, and freshwater populations, stickleback are exposed to oil in a variety of aquatic environments. We aimed to understand fish recovery following removal of crude oil. Stickleback were exposed to Alaska North Slope crude oil and then were moved to water without crude oil for two weeks of recovery. Measurements of growth and immunity were taken before and after the recovery period. We found that crude oil effected different developmental pathways independently. Crude oil significantly impacted snout-vent length and eye diameter, but not swim bladder length or area, nor expression of IL1B and TNF genes. Stickleback fish were unable to recover from exposure after being transferred to clean water for two-weeks. This is the first study to examine the effect crude oil has on early stages of stickleback development and potential recovery. The results suggest larval and juvenile stickleback exposed to crude oil need longer than two-weeks to recover if they are able to recover at all.
